title: Weekly Briefing: Workers Are Managing AI Without Raises, Andreessen Horowitz Rethinks College, and the Great Iced Coffee Interview Debate
author: Jacob Morgan
summary: Jacob Morgan's Future Ready Leadership Weekly Briefing picks three stories about the talent system and adds a CHRO-oriented commentary to each. The first covers a Business Insider report that employees are quietly becoming managers of AI agents, with a BCG survey showing 47% spend more time managing AI than doing the work and only 36% receiving relevant upskilling. The second looks at Andreessen Horowitz's new academy with no grades, tests or homework, and asks whether a degree should remain such a strong proxy for talent. The third uses a viral recruiter TikTok about iced coffee in interviews to question what "professional" means and which hiring signals actually predict performance. Across all three, Morgan presses employers to align titles, pay and hiring practices with what they say they value. The issue closes with a note on a podcast conversation with Jill Penrose of The J.M. Smucker Co. about focusing AI investment on differentiated business value.
points: Employees who delegate to, review and correct AI agents are performing management work, so organizations need to define what counts as AI management, how many agents one person can supervise, and whether it should affect pay and promotion.

The BCG figures (47% spending more time managing AI than doing the work, 72% reporting changed skill demands, 36% upskilled) show the upskilling gap is the practical risk behind AI productivity gains.
The a16z academy is too small to replace universities, but it tests whether employers who say they want skills-based hiring will actually hire people who demonstrate capability without a degree.

The iced coffee debate is really about unwritten professionalism rules, and Morgan argues a good hiring process should measure ability to succeed in the role rather than reward guessing the interviewer's preferences.
quotes: As companies deploy more AI agents, employees are increasingly responsible for configuring them, giving them work, reviewing what they produce, correcting mistakes, and deciding when the output is good enough to use.

If someone is responsible for delegating work to agents, evaluating their performance, fixing problems, and taking accountability for the final result, then their role has changed whether the org chart acknowledges it or not.
Otherwise companies risk celebrating AI productivity while quietly loading more responsibility onto employees.

Fifty students obviously do not represent an alternative to the entire university system. But I think the experiment is worth watching because it goes directly at something employers have been saying for years: they want skills, experience, judgment, and evidence that someone can actually do the work.
We talk constantly about skills-based hiring. Programs like this are a chance to see whether employers really mean it.
The coffee itself is almost beside the point. What people are really arguing about is professionalism.
If someone carrying an iced latte meaningfully changes how you evaluate their intelligence, work ethic, or capability, what exactly are you measuring?
A good hiring process should make it easier to identify whether someone can succeed in the role, not reward the candidate who is best at guessing every unwritten rule.
